Theme: Risk Assessment Tools in Forensic Psychiatry

For each description, select the CORRECT RISK ASSESSMENT TOOL:

A. HCR-20
B. PCL-R
C. VRAG
D. SORAG
E. RSVP
F. START
G. Static-99
H. H10
I. S5
J. The Dundrum Toolkit
K. Risk Matrix 2000
L. SARA

Stem 1: A 30-item structured professional judgement tool assessing GENERAL VIOLENCE risk, with sections on Historical, Clinical, and Risk Management factors. The most widely used SPJ tool.
options: A 20-item SCALE (not a risk assessment tool) measuring PSYCHOPATHY using Factor 1 (interpersonal/affective) and Factor 2 (antisocial lifestyle) scores. Scores range 0-40; cut-off for psychopathy in the UK is usually 25 or 30.
An ACTUARIAL tool for SEXUAL violence recidivism using 10 static items (all historical). Provides a numerical probability of reoffending. Used for sex offender risk assessment.

A risk formulation and MANAGEMENT planning tool designed for SEXUAL VIOLENCE that includes 22 items across 5 domains. It is a STRUCTURED PROFESSIONAL JUDGEMENT tool.

For each statement below, select the correct tool from the list above

A) For item A
A 22-item SPJ tool for SEXUAL VIOLENCE risk assessment, formulation, and scenario planning. The preferred tool for sexual violence risk.
distractors_rationale: This is the correct answer. Forensic risk assessment tools — HIGH-YIELD: GENERAL VIOLENCE: HCR-20 (SPJ) — most important. VRAG (actuarial). SEXUAL VIOLENCE: RSVP (SPJ — preferred). Static-99, Risk Matrix 2000 (actuarial). PSYCHOPATHY: PCL-R (semi-structured interview + file review). STALKING: Stalking Risk Profile. FIRESETTING: Firesetting Risk Assessment Tool. VIOLENCE in psychiatric patients: HCR-20. DUNDRUM TOOLKIT: for assessing readiness for movement through forensic services (from high secure to community). START (Short Term Assessment of Risk and Treatability): a 20-item SPJ tool for short-term risk assessment in mental health settings (violence, self-harm, suicide, absconding, self-neglect). SPJ tools are preferred OVER actuarial because they: (1) Can incorporate case-specific dynamic risk factors; (2) Guide risk MANAGEMENT (not just prediction); (3) Are more defensible in court; (4) Are more acceptable to clinicians. BPS (Best Practice in Risk Assessment and Management): the Department of Health guidance recommends structured risk assessment using SPJ tools.

HCR-20 (Webster et al., 1997). The HCR-20 is the most widely used STRUCTURED PROFESSIONAL JUDGEMENT (SPJ) tool for GENERAL VIOLENCE risk assessment. 20 items across 3 scales: H (HISTORICAL — 10 items: past violence, young age at first violence, relationship instability, employment, substance use, major mental illness, psychopathy, early maladjustment, personality disorder, prior supervision failure); C (CLINICAL — 5 items: insight, negative attitudes, active symptoms, impulsivity, treatment non-response); R (RISK MANAGEMENT — 5 future-oriented items: plans, exposure to destabilisers, lack of personal support, non-compliance with remediation, stress). Each item rated 0-2 (No, Maybe, Yes). The HCR-20 does NOT produce a numerical probability — it guides clinical judgement about the nature, severity, imminence, and likelihood of violence. It is updated as Version 3 (2013). The HCR-20 is recommended by NICE for assessing violence risk in psychiatric patients.

The PCL-R (Hare, 1991, 2003) is a 20-item CLINICIAN-RATED SCALE that measures PSYCHOPATHY, not risk per se. It is a risk FACTOR (one item in the HCR-20). Factor 1: Interpersonal/Affective (glibness/superficial charm, grandiose sense of self-worth, pathological lying, lack of remorse, shallow affect, callous/lack of empathy, failure to accept responsibility). Factor 2: Antisocial Lifestyle (need for stimulation, parasitic lifestyle, poor behavioural control, early behavioural problems, lack of realistic goals, impulsivity, irresponsibility, many short-term marital relationships, juvenile delinquency, revocation of conditional release). The PCL-R is the gold standard for assessing psychopathy. Cut-off: UK 25/40 (North America 30/40). The PCL-R is NOT a risk assessment tool — it assesses a trait that is associated with risk.

STATIC-99 (G) or RISK MATRIX 2000 (K) — both are ACTUARIAL tools for sexual recidivism. STATIC-99: 10 items (male sex, prior sexual offences, prior non-sexual violence, non-related victims, male victims, never married, stranger victims, unrelated victims, age under 25, ever lived with a partner for 2+ years). RISK MATRIX 2000: three scales (criminal history, sexual offence history, victim type). STATIC-99R is the updated version. The SORAG (Sex Offender Risk Appraisal Guide) is another actuarial tool. However, the RSVP is the STRUCTURED PROFESSIONAL JUDGEMENT tool preferred by the Royal College of Psychiatrists for sexual violence risk.

RSVP — Risk of Sexual Violence Protocol (Hart et al., 2003). The RSVP is a 22-item SPJ tool for sexual violence risk. It has FIVE DOMAINS: (1) Sexual Violence History; (2) Psychological Adjustment (sexual deviance, cognitive distortion, mental disorder); (3) Mental Disorder (psychopathy, major mental illness, substance misuse, violent ideation); (4) Social Adjustment (intimacy problems, negative attitudes, conflict, poor social skills); (5) Manageability (treatment engagement, supervision, insight, motivation). The RSVP provides a framework for CASE FORMULATION, RISK SCENARIO PLANNING (identifying 'worst-case' scenarios), and RISK MANAGEMENT PLANNING. It does NOT produce an overall numerical score — it guides professional judgement. It is the preferred SPJ tool for sexual violence.
teaching_point: Forensic risk assessment tools — HIGH-YIELD: GENERAL VIOLENCE: HCR-20 (SPJ) — most important. VRAG (actuarial). SEXUAL VIOLENCE: RSVP (SPJ — preferred). Static-99, Risk Matrix 2000 (actuarial). PSYCHOPATHY: PCL-R (semi-structured interview + file review). STALKING: Stalking Risk Profile. FIRESETTING: Firesetting Risk Assessment Tool. VIOLENCE in psychiatric patients: HCR-20. DUNDRUM TOOLKIT: for assessing readiness for movement through forensic services (from high secure to community). START (Short Term Assessment of Risk and Treatability): a 20-item SPJ tool for short-term risk assessment in mental health settings (violence, self-harm, suicide, absconding, self-neglect). SPJ tools are preferred OVER actuarial because they: (1) Can incorporate case-specific dynamic risk factors; (2) Guide risk MANAGEMENT (not just prediction); (3) Are more defensible in court; (4) Are more acceptable to clinicians. BPS (Best Practice in Risk Assessment and Management): the Department of Health guidance recommends structured risk assessment using SPJ tools.
source: Webster CD et al. (1997) HCR-20; Hare RD (2003) PCL-R; Hart SD et al. (2003) RSVP; NICE guidance on violence

stem: A 27-year-old man with Asperger's syndrome (mild autism, average IQ) is charged with possessing indecent images of children. He has no previous convictions. He lives alone, is socially isolated, and spends most of his time on the internet. Psychiatric assessment reveals: (1) No paraphilic disorder (he is not sexually attracted to children — images were part of a 'collection' behaviour); (2) No evidence of contact offending; (3) Limited understanding of the social and legal implications of his actions. What is the MOST important factor in formulating risk and recommending disposal?
options: He should receive a prison sentence of significant length to protect the public

The formulation should consider his AUTISM-RELATED VULNERABILITIES (social naivety, repetitive interests, literal interpretation, lack of understanding of consequences) alongside risk-specific factors — he may benefit from a HOSPITAL ORDER (Section 37) or community order with specialist supervision rather than prison
He should be sectioned under the MHA for treatment of autism
He should be found not guilty by reason of insanity
He should be placed on the Sex Offenders Register indefinitely
distractors_rationale: A prison sentence without addressing the underlying formulation may not be appropriate. The court must consider whether there is a mental disorder that warrants treatment.

CORRECT. This is a complex forensic case requiring a NUANCED FORMULATION. The individual has: (1) AUTISM SPECTRUM DISORDER — associated with social naivety, repetitive behaviours (including internet use/ collectings), difficulty understanding social/legal boundaries, and circumscribed interests (may focus on the images as an interest rather than a paraphilic drive). (2) NO PARAPHILIA — this is not a sexual attraction to children; the behaviour has a different motivation (collecting, fascination with the images as objects). (3) LOW RISK OF CONTACT SEXUAL OFFENDING — sexual offences by people with ASD are less common than in the general offending population. (4) VULNERABILITY — his social isolation and naivety make him vulnerable in prison (victimisation). APPROPRIATE DISPOSAL: The court should consider: (a) A psychiatric report exploring the link between ASD and the offending; (b) A MENTAL HEALTH TREATMENT REQUIREMENT as part of a community order (if the MHA does not apply — Asperger's is not a 'treatable' mental disorder under the MHA unless there is a comorbid condition); (c) Specialist forensic ASD services for assessment and guidance; (d) The probation service and MAPPA (Multi-Agency Public Protection Arrangements) should be involved. Prison may be INCREDIBLY HARMFUL for someone with ASD and may not address the underlying risk.
ASD alone is not a mental disorder 'of a nature or degree' warranting detention under the MHA unless there is a comorbid mental illness (depression, psychosis).

A defence of insanity requires a 'defect of reason from disease of the mind' such that the person did not know the nature and quality of the act OR that it was wrong. This person may have understood the ACT (downloading images) but not fully appreciated its WRONGFULNESS due to ASD. However, this would be decided by the court with expert evidence and is not automatic.
Registration on the Sex Offenders Register is a court decision, not a psychiatric decision, and would depend on the nature of the offence.
teaching_point: ASD and forensic psychiatry — HIGH-YIELD emerging topic: (1) PREVALENCE: ASD is OVERREPRESENTED in forensic populations (especially in those with arson, indecent images, and stalking offences). (2) RISK FACTORS: social naivety, repetitive interests, poor understanding of consequences, difficulty reading social cues, co-morbid mental illness, victim of bullying, social isolation. (3) OFFENDING PATTERNS in ASD: indecent image offences (collecting behaviour rather than paedophilic drive), stalking (misinterpretation of social cues), arson (fascination with fire), computer-related offences. (4) RISK ASSESSMENT: tools need ADAPTATION for ASD (the HCR-20 may capture autistic behaviours as 'negative attitudes' or 'impulsivity' when they are ASD characteristics, not risk factors). (5) DISPOSAL: hospital order under MHA may be appropriate if there is comorbid treatable mental disorder; community supervision with specialist input; MAPPA. (6) Autism Act 2009: statutory guidance requires services to meet the needs of autistic people in the criminal justice system. The 'TRAIN' framework (National Autistic Society) provides guidance for police and courts.
source: Howlin P (2004) Autism and offending; Allen D et al. (2008) Offending in ASD; NICE CG170; Autism Act 2009

stem: A 34-year-old woman with moderate learning disability and epilepsy is referred due to worsening agitation, aggression, and insomnia over 6 weeks. She cannot explain why she feels this way. Her support workers report she has been hitting staff and biting herself. She is on carbamazepine 400mg BD. Physical examination and routine bloods (FBC, U&Es, LFTs, TFTs, glucose) are NORMAL. Which of the following should be done NEXT?
options: Start risperidone 0.5mg daily for challenging behaviour
Increase carbamazepine — she may be having complex partial seizures
Arrange a COMPREHENSIVE PAIN ASSESSMENT and dental review — dental pain/abscess is a very common cause of behavioural change in LD and is often missed
Admit to a psychiatric intensive care unit
distractors_rationale: Starting antipsychotic without understanding the cause is not first-line. NICE NG11: 'Do not use antipsychotics for challenging behaviour unless there is evidence of a mental disorder or the behaviour is clearly related to it.' Behaviour is COMMUNICATION in LD — the first step is to find out what the person is trying to communicate.
Increasing carbamazepine without evidence of seizures is not indicated. Her epilepsy is well-controlled.

CORRECT. PAIN is the SINGLE MOST COMMON cause of acute behavioural change in people with LD who cannot communicate verbally. Dental pain, tooth abscess, ear infection, UTI, constipation, headache, menstrual pain, fractures — all can present as aggression, agitation, and self-injury. In this patient: (1) Dental pain is ESPECIALLY common in people with LD (poor oral hygiene, access to dental care issues, bruxism). (2) UTI is also very common. (3) Constipation (especially with carbamazepine — which can cause constipation). (4) The 6-week duration suggests a PERSISTENT pain problem (like a dental abscess, constipation, or menstrual issues). MANAGEMENT: (1) FULL PHYSICAL EXAM (including oral cavity, abdomen, ears). (2) DENTAL REVIEW (often missed — arrange immediately). (3) Urinalysis and MSU. (4) REVIEW of medications (side effects). (5) Pain assessment using an ADAPTED PAIN SCALE (e.g., PAINAD — Pain Assessment in Advanced Dementia scale — adapted for LD). Only after physical causes are excluded should psychiatric diagnoses or medication for behaviour be considered.
Admission is not first-line without acute medical or psychiatric risk that cannot be managed in the community.

Benzodiazepines are not indicated for chronic agitation in LD — they can cause paradoxical disinhibition, falls, tolerance, and dependence. They may be used short-term for acute crisis but not as ongoing treatment.
teaching_point: Pain and behavioural change in LD — the NUMBER ONE cause: People with LD are at HIGHER RISK of: (1) Dental disease (poor oral hygiene, access issues, dietary factors); (2) Gastrointestinal problems (GERD, constipation, dysphagia); (3) Epilepsy and post-ictal changes; (4) Sensory impairments; (5) Fractures (lower bone density, falls); (6) Menstrual pain (dysmenorrhea). The 'BEHAVIOUR IS COMMUNICATION' principle: Agitation, aggression, self-injury, or withdrawal may be the ONLY way a person with LD can communicate PAIN, FEAR, FRUSTRATION, or ILLNESS. Assessment approach (NICE NG11): (1) Treat possible physical causes FIRST (before assuming psychiatric cause). (2) Consider: pain, infection, constipation, hunger, thirst, sensory deprivation, side effects of medication, environmental factors (noise, over/under-stimulation, staff changes). (3) Use COLLATERAL HISTORY from carers and family. (4) Use formal PAIN ASSESSMENT TOOLS (PAINAD, FLACC, NCCPC). The STOMP (Stopping Over-Medication) campaign aims to reduce inappropriate psychotropic prescribing for challenging behaviour in LD.
source: NICE NG11: Challenging behaviour and LD; NICE guideline on LD; STOMP campaign (NHS England)
